one_liner: Header-only C++17 vector without zero-init, exceptions, or a real allocator; beats std::vector on trivial-type push_back workloads.
what_it_does: fast_vector is a single-header replacement for std::vector<T> that skips value-initialization on reserve/resize, allocates via malloc/realloc/free instead of an allocator, and replaces exception-based error handling with assert() calls that compile out in release builds. The public API covers push_back, emplace_back, pop_back, resize, reserve, shrink_to_fit, clear, front/back/operator[], and begin()/end() iteration, but has no insert(), erase(), at(), swap(), or allocator support (a user opened issue #1 asking for insert/erase). It is not a strict drop-in: trivial elements are left uninitialized rather than value-initialized, and there is no exception path for out-of-range access.
how_it_is_fast: For trivial T, reserve/resize skip the construct/destruct loops std::vector runs and grow via realloc() in place instead of malloc+copy+free; push_back writes trivial elements by assignment rather than placement-new. Bounds and precondition checks are assert()-based, so unlike std::vector's exception-safety machinery they cost nothing under NDEBUG. There is no SIMD, custom allocator, or branchless logic involved — the win is purely from removing zero-initialization and object-lifetime bookkeeping that trivial types don't need.
when_to_use: Hot loops doing push_back/emplace_back on many trivial (POD) elements where leaving memory uninitialized (instead of value-initialized) is acceptable
Codebases already built assertions-first/exceptions-off (e.g. game or low-latency style code) that want realloc-based growth instead of malloc+copy+free
Header-only vendoring into a C++17 project where pulling in a full container library is undesirable
Non-trivial types specifically via emplace_back (~1.3x measured) rather than push_back+pop_back or reserve+push_back, which show little to no win for non-trivial T
when_not_to_use: Any code that copies or copy-assigns a fast_vector<T> where sizeof(T) > 1: the copy ctor/operator= call memcpy(dst, src, other.m_size) using element count instead of byte count, under-copying data (open issue #2, unresolved since 2019)
operator=(const fast_vector&) never frees the destination's existing allocation before overwriting the pointer, leaking the old buffer on reassignment
Anything needing insert()/erase() at arbitrary positions, at(), swap(), comparison operators, or initializer-list construction — none exist (open issue #1)
Release builds where out-of-bounds safety matters: assert() is a no-op under NDEBUG, so operator[]/front/back/pop_back have zero bounds checking in release
Non-trivial-type reserve+push_back workloads specifically: the README's own numbers show std::vector 88,303ns vs fast_vector 88,671ns, i.e. no measured win

integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (stated in README); benchmarked with Visual Studio 2017, no other compiler/version documented
integration.platforms: any — portable C++17, no platform-specific intrinsics or code observed in fast_vector.h
integration.thread_safety: not documented; no internal synchronization in the header, same external-locking burden as std::vector
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: same core method names (push_back/emplace_back/pop_back/resize/reserve/iterators) as std::vector, but missing insert/erase/at/swap/allocator support, no value-initialization, and two unresolved correctness bugs (wrong memcpy size, leak in copy-assignment) make it unsafe as a literal find-and-replace for std::vector

gotchas: Copy constructor and copy-assignment memcpy the wrong byte count (other.m_size instead of other.m_size * sizeof(T)) for trivial T larger than 1 byte — filed as issue #2, still open at last commit
Copy-assignment operator leaks the destination's prior allocation: it never calls std::free on the old m_data before reassigning the pointer
grow_factor is advertised as 'modifiable' but is a static constexpr size_type = 2 baked into the header, not a template or runtime parameter — changing it means editing the source
reserve()/resize() assert preconditions (new_cap > capacity; count != size) that are silently skipped in release builds rather than raising an error
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over plf::colony/plf::list/veque/EASTL only when you want a minimal, header-only, std::vector-shaped container purely for trivial-type push_back-heavy code and can tolerate its two open correctness bugs; veque and plf::colony/plf::list report larger, more thoroughly benchmarked wins for their respective access patterns, and EASTL is a more mature, allocator-aware drop-in that fast_vector doesn't match.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel i7-4720HQ (Visual Studio 2017, MSVC STL, Windows 10), Google Benchmark over 10,000 elements showed fast_vector roughly 1.4-2.1x faster than std::vector for trivial-type push_back, reserve+push_back, and push_back+pop_back, but only about 1.0-1.3x for non-trivial types, with non-trivial reserve+push_back essentially a wash (88,303ns vs 88,671ns).
status_note: Abandoned since its last commit on 2019-04-20, with two unresolved open issues (a copy-constructor memcpy bug and a missing insert/erase request); MIT-licensed, 21 stars, and small enough — one header — to vendor and patch yourself.
